summary: Describes a security problem with IPv6-in-IPv4 automatic tunnels, where an attacker exploits mismatches between IPv4 and IPv6 routing state to form a routing loop that can amplify traffic for denial-of-service attacks. It explains the root causes and proposes mitigations.

eli5.summary: If two signposts each point to the other, a traveler walks in circles forever. An attacker can create such a loop for internet packets and use it to flood someone. This explains how and how to stop it.

questions: ipv6 automatic tunnel routing loop attack
how to prevent tunnel routing loops
subtitle: A routing loop vulnerability in IPv6-in-IPv4 automatic tunnels and how to stop it.

tldr.problem: IPv6-in-IPv4 automatic tunnels (6to4, ISATAP, 6rd) are vulnerable to routing loops when two tunnel routers are unaware of each other's configurations, allowing an attacker to craft packets that bounce between them indefinitely.
tldr.mechanism: An attacker sends a packet with a spoofed source address to one tunnel router, which decapsulates and forwards it to another tunnel router, which encapsulates it back, creating a loop. The loop persists until the packet's hop count expires, during which time the packet can be replicated for amplification attacks.
tldr.outcome: The RFC documents the vulnerability (no known malicious exploits at publication) and proposes five categories of mitigation: endpoint verification, operational separation of tunnels, and address validation checks.

facts.label: Attack termination
facts.value: When IPv6 hop limit reaches zero

facts.label: Known exploits at publication
facts.value: None, but accidental misconfiguration can trigger the vulnerability

today: RFC 6324 is Informational. The document highlighted a real vulnerability in the design of IPv6 automatic tunnels. While no malicious exploits were known at publication, the mitigations described remain relevant for deployments using 6to4, ISATAP, or 6rd.

sections.title: IPv6 Automatic Tunnels and the Vulnerability
sections.content:
IPv6 automatic tunnels are tunnels that carry IPv6 packets through IPv4 networks without requiring manual configuration of each tunnel endpoint. The most common types are 6to4 (IPv6 addresses start with 2002::, with the IPv4 address embedded), ISATAP (Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol), and 6rd (IPv6 Rapid Deployment).

All three use protocol-41 encapsulation: IPv6 packets are wrapped inside IPv4 headers so they can traverse IPv4 networks. The tunnel router on the other side unwraps them and forwards the IPv6 packet onward.

The vulnerability arises because tunnel routers make an implicit assumption: the destination IPv6 address embedded in a packet is always a valid node reachable via that tunnel. This assumption can be violated when an attacker crafts a packet that exploits the gap between IPv4 and IPv6 routing state.
sections.eli5: Tunnels carry IPv6 messages through IPv4 networks automatically by embedding the IPv4 address in the IPv6 address. Each tunnel router assumes a message destined to a certain IPv6 address can be reached through its tunnel, but this assumption can be tricked.

sections.title: How the Attack Works
sections.content:
Imagine two tunnel routers, R1 and R2, each serving a different IPv6 tunnel prefix and each having an IPv4 address in the same IPv4 network. An attacker sends a packet to R2 with:

  • IPv6 source address derived from R1's tunnel prefix and R2's IPv4 address
  • IPv6 destination address derived from R2's tunnel prefix and R1's IPv4 address

R2 receives the IPv6 packet and encapsulates it into IPv4, sending it to R1's IPv4 address. R1 receives the encapsulated packet, recognizes the source address as valid for its tunnel (because the embedded IPv4 address matches R2's), and decapsulates it. Since the destination is not part of R1's prefix, R1 forwards the IPv6 packet back to the native IPv6 network. The packet is routed back to R2, and the loop begins again.

The loop terminates only when the IPv6 hop limit field reaches zero, but until then the packet bounces between R1 and R2. An attacker can amplify traffic by sending many such packets simultaneously.
sections.eli5: The attacker tricks R2 into sending to R1, R1 into sending back to R2, over and over. The packet goes round and round until it expires.

sections.title: Endpoint Verification Mitigations
sections.content:
One approach is to verify that a node actually exists before forwarding to it. Neighbor cache checking maintains a list of known IPv6 hosts reachable via the tunnel. The router only forwards packets if the destination is in the cache or performs a reachability check first.

Known IPv4 address checking is simpler: the router is configured with a list of authorized IPv4 addresses for the tunnel. It discards packets with source or destination addresses embedding unauthorized IPv4 addresses. This works well for small, static tunnel deployments like ISATAP in an enterprise.
sections.eli5: Keep a list of real computers you know about. Send packets only to them. Or have a list of which IPv4 addresses are allowed, and reject the others.

sections.title: Operational Mitigations
sections.content:
The simplest fix is to prevent the attack configuration from existing in the first place. Single router per IPv4 network: if there is only one tunnel router in a bounded IPv4 network (like a home network), the attack cannot occur because there is no second router to loop with.

Avoiding IPv4 protocol-41 packets: filtering out protocol-41 packets on untrusted interfaces cuts off the IPv4 network as a shared link between tunnels, though this breaks legitimate IPv6 tunneling.

Comprehensive router list: if a tunnel router knows about all other tunnel routers in its IPv4 region, it can filter out packets from or to unknown routers, preventing the loop between unknowns.

Avoiding on-link prefixes: for ISATAP, if routers do not advertise non-link-local prefixes and hosts acquire addresses via DHCPv6 instead, the router cannot initiate the loop.
sections.eli5: Don't have two tunnels in the same place. Or ignore tunnel traffic on untrusted links. Or tell routers only about the routers they should know. Or don't let routers advertise addresses they don't really own.

sections.title: Address Validation Mitigations
sections.content:
Tunnel routers can perform source and destination address checks: when forwarding a packet into a tunnel interface, discard it if the source address embeds one of the router's own IPv4 addresses. Similarly, when receiving a packet on a tunnel interface, discard it if the destination address embeds one of the router's addresses.

For example, a 6to4 router discards packets with source addresses in the 2002: range if the embedded IPv4 address is the router's own. An ISATAP router discards packets with destination addresses with an ISATAP suffix if the embedded IPv4 address is one of its configured addresses.

The RFC also describes a known IPv6 prefix check: if the router is configured with a list of legitimate IPv6 prefixes in its IPv4 region, it can apply address checks only to addresses that embed private IPv4 addresses and match those prefixes, reducing false positives.
sections.eli5: Routers can check their packet addresses: if a source or destination looks like it was sent from or to the router itself, throw it away.

sections.title: Best Practices and Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC makes recommendations in order of effectiveness:

  1. Operationally eliminate the attack by configuring networks to prevent the vulnerable scenario (single tunnel, single border router)
  2. Use neighbor cache checking if you maintain a coherent cache of all legitimate endpoints
  3. Use neighbor reachability checking where feasible
  4. Use known IPv4 address checking for small static tunnel deployments
  5. Avoid relying on destination and source address checks alone, as they do not work against 6rd routers

The document notes that tunnels may be deployed in various environments (service provider, enterprise, etc.) and operators should select mitigations appropriate to their specific scenario.
sections.eli5: First, build the network so the attack cannot happen. If you can't, check that the other end is real. If you can't, check the addresses. Last resort: make sure routers don't talk to themselves.
